summary.text: Coral bleaching is the process in which corals turn white after losing their symbiotic algae and photosynthetic pigments.
Single-celled partners called zooxanthellae live in coral tissue and supply up to 90 percent of its energy, so a coral that expels them may begin to starve.
Rising ocean temperatures from climate change are the leading cause, and large bleaching events can devastate entire reef ecosystems.

items.prompt: After a hot summer, divers find a once-colourful reef gone ghostly white. What has the coral lost?

options.label: Its hard skeleton, which dissolved away
The tiny partners living in its tissue
A coat of sand that usually covers it
Its outer skin, which peeled off in heat

items.explain: Under stress the coral consumes or expels the zooxanthellae that live in its tissues and give it colour, leaving it pale or white.

items.prompt: A bleached coral is still alive, yet it may begin to starve. Why?

options.label: Fish stop bringing it scraps of food
White coral cannot catch any prey
It lost partners that made most of its energy
Warm water holds no food at all

items.explain: The zooxanthellae supply up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis, so after expelling them the coral may starve.

items.prompt: A bleached coral makes it through the heat. What has to happen for it to recover?

options.label: Its partners must move back in and photosynthesize again
It must grow a fresh skeleton from scratch
Seaweed must cover it to shade it
It must drift to cooler, deeper water

items.explain: To recover, the zooxanthellae have to re-enter the coral polyps' tissues and restart photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Two reefs face the same hot spell: one sits in warm, shallow, still water, the other where strong currents flow. Which tends to suffer more bleaching?

options.label: The reef in strong currents
Both suffer exactly the same
Neither, since heat alone cannot bleach coral
The reef in shallow, still water

items.explain: Reefs in warm, shallow water with low water flow have been more affected than reefs in areas with higher water flow.

items.prompt: Coral polyps starve and die after bleaching, leaving their skeletons behind. What happens to the reef next?

options.label: New polyps sprout from the skeletons within weeks
The skeletons slowly regain their colour
Algae take over and block new coral growth
The skeletons harden into stronger rock

items.explain: Dead hard corals leave calcium carbonate skeletons that algae take over, blocking regrowth; eventually the skeletons erode and the reef collapses.

items.prompt: If global warming reaches 2 °C, how often is bleaching predicted to strike the Great Barrier Reef?

options.label: About once every fifty years
Roughly every other year
About once a decade
Never again, as corals adapt

items.explain: Bleaching is predicted three times a decade at 1.5 °C of warming, rising to every other year at 2 °C.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Coral bleaching is what happens when corals turn white because they lose the algae that live with them in partnership, along with photosynthetic pigments. A bleached coral is a coral under stress. It is more likely to starve or fall sick, and it may die.

paragraphs.heading: A partnership under strain
paragraphs.text: Reef-building corals in tropical seas rely on a close partnership with zooxanthellae, tiny single-celled organisms that live inside the coral's tissue and give it its colour. Through photosynthesis the zooxanthellae feed the coral, which counts for a lot in clear tropical water that holds few nutrients. In return the coral hands them the carbon dioxide and ammonium they need to photosynthesise. The zooxanthellae can meet as much as 90 percent of the coral's energy needs.

paragraphs.heading: How a coral bleaches
paragraphs.text: Bad conditions, such as water that is unusually warm or cool, strong light, or some microbial diseases, can break the partnership apart. To survive in the short term, the coral polyp then eats or expels its zooxanthellae, and it turns pale or fully white. Under mild stress some corals look blue, pink, purple or yellow instead, because their own pigments stay or even increase; this is called colourful bleaching. With its partners gone, the coral may start to starve.

paragraphs.heading: Recovery or collapse
paragraphs.text: A coral can get through a short upset, but its odds fall if the stress goes on. To recover, zooxanthellae have to move back into the polyps and start photosynthesising again. If the polyps starve to death instead, they rot away, leaving hard skeletons of calcium carbonate that algae take over, which stops new coral from growing. In time those skeletons wear away and the reef collapses.

paragraphs.heading: The role of warming seas
paragraphs.text: Stresses such as shifts in temperature, light, salt or nutrients can all trigger bleaching, but the leading cause is ocean warming driven by climate change. Local triggers cause local bleaching, while the huge events of recent years were set off by global warming. Marine heatwaves linked to the El Niño Southern Oscillation are among the main causes of widespread bleaching and coral death. The oceans are also becoming more acidic as they absorb carbon dioxide from the air, which harms corals too.

paragraphs.heading: A worldwide crisis
paragraphs.text: On 15 April 2024, NOAA confirmed that the fourth global coral bleaching event was under way, the largest yet. Between January 2023 and September 2025, heat stress strong enough to bleach coral reached about 84.4% of the world's reef area, and bleaching was recorded in 83 or more countries and territories. On the Great Barrier Reef, bleaching in 2016 killed between 29 and 50 percent of the coral. Such events can wreck whole reef ecosystems, hurting wildlife and the coastal people who rely on reefs for food, tourism and shelter from storm surges.
